{"id": "7:150/q20", "question": "How do sources assess Moses' treatment of Aaron?", "turns_on": "The significance of custom, prophetic impeccability, sincere zeal, and claims of humiliating discipline.", "positions": [{"id": "7:150/q20/p1", "position": "The seizure could be read as humiliating or disciplining Aaron.", "reasons": "WAHIDI-WAJIZ (author): Aaron asks Moses not to let the calf worshippers rejoice over him by striking or humiliating him, or count him among the wrongdoers. KASHSHAF-FULL (author): Moses is asked not to do what the enemies hoped for by humiliating or mistreating Aaron; a reading instead addresses the enemies, forbidding them to rejoice. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (author): The people who had weakened Aaron were the calf worshippers, and they had humiliated him. RAZI-FULL (الطاعنون في عصمة الأنبياء): Those who challenge prophetic impeccability say Moses pulled Aaron’s head toward him to humiliate and belittle him. QURTUBI-FULL (العلماء): The fourth view says Moses embraced Aaron to learn what had happened; Aaron feared Israel would mistake it for humiliation. QURTUBI-FULL (العلماء): A second interpretation says Moses wanted to whisper about the tablets revealed during the private conversation and conceal them from the Israelites; Aaron objected lest the gesture look humiliating. NASAFI-FULL (author): The enemies are the calf worshippers; Moses should not do what they wish by humiliating or harming Aaron, or treat him as one of the wrongdoers by sharing his anger with them. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): One view says Moses grabbed Aaron only to tell him privately that the tablets had descended during his communion, and Aaron stopped him lest the Israelites mistake the private exchange for humiliation. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Another view says Moses pulled Aaron close to learn what happened; Aaron feared the Israelites would think Moses was humiliating him and explained their oppression. BIQAI-FULL (author): Aaron says the people intimidated him and nearly killed him for objecting; he asks Moses not to let their enemies rejoice at his humiliation or count him among the wrongdoers. BURSEVI (author): Moses threw down the tablets of the Torah and pulled Aaron by the hair toward himself in reproach, not to humiliate him, supposing he had failed to restrain the people; Aaron was older, gentle, and loved by the Israelites. ALUSI-FULL (author): Moses did not intend to humiliate Aaron; the physical reproach addressed what seemed a failure of duty under his leadership, born of religious zeal. ALUSI-FULL (author): Aaron says the people overpowered and humiliated him and disregarded him because he had few supporters. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): Throwing the tablets was not punishment of the people, since tablets containing what would reform them could not appropriately be treated as prophetic discipline.
